opus-5.5.text:
That was a project I did with Danyel Fisher a long time ago, and it taught me something I keep coming back to: people don't see a visualization as a pile of individual marks. They see shapes, clusters, and regions, and they see them at several scales at once. The question we asked was simple: if you blur an image at different levels, which structures survive? We found that this was a surprisingly good proxy for what a person would group together when they glance at a chart.

The practical lesson was that the designer isn't fully in control of what the viewer sees. You can carefully encode some variable in color or position, but if the eye fuses a set of marks into a blob at a coarser scale, that blob is what people will talk about. Sometimes it's the pattern you wanted, and sometimes it's an accident of layout that people then read meaning into. So part of designing a good visualization is anticipating those emergent groupings and either taking advantage of them or breaking them up.

The other thing it taught me is humility about formal models of perception. A fairly crude computational model got you a lot of the way, which was encouraging. But the remaining gap, where context, expectations, and the viewer's own questions shape what they see, was where much of the interesting behavior lived. That's stayed with me: you can model the low-level perceptual machinery reasonably well, but understanding how people *use* a visualization means watching what they actually do with it. A lot of my later work, on social and public visualization tools, came from wanting to see that in the wild rather than in the lab.

r001.rationale: The candidate describes blurring an image at different levels as a proxy for grouping, but does not identify computer-vision scale-space techniques or say they formalized designers’ intuitions.

r002.rationale: It says a crude model captured much of low-level perception but left a gap involving context and expectations; it does not state that Wattenberg’s understanding of vision at the time was insufficient to simulate a viewer’s experience.

r003.rationale: The candidate says observing what people do with visualizations matters, but does not compare a brief conversation and observation with applying a sophisticated mathematical model to the image.

fable-5.1.text:
That's a fun question, because it goes back to work I did with a collaborator, Marek Fiser, that was in some ways pretty far from what I do now. The idea was pretty simple: when you look at a scatterplot, or really any image, you don't just see a set of dots. You see clusters, you see trends, you see outliers. Your visual system is doing a kind of grouping. And the interesting thing is that the grouping happens at multiple scales at once. You might see three big clumps, and inside one of those clumps you see a little substructure, and so on.

So we tried to build a model of that, a sort of multiscale description of how a picture gets carved up into groups, and the way it related to what people actually reported seeing when we showed them the images.

What it taught me, honestly, was a little humbling. The first lesson was that "what's in the data" and "what people see" are two really different things, and the gap is bigger than you'd like. You can have a perfectly honest chart that's technically showing a correlation, and people just don't perceive it, because the visual organization is pulling their attention somewhere else. The eye grabs onto a cluster or a gap or a stray point, and that becomes the story, regardless of what you, the designer, thought the story was.

The second lesson is that this grouping is doing most of the work. When someone looks at a visualization and says "I get it," what they mostly mean is that their perceptual system has already chunked the picture into a small number of objects they can reason about. If the chunking matches the structure you care about, the visualization feels effortless. If it doesn't, no amount of labeling or annotation really saves you. So a lot of what I now think of as good visualization design is really just getting the perceptual grouping to line up with the semantic grouping.

And the third thing, which I think about constantly now that I spend a lot of time looking at machine learning systems, is that it made me suspicious of any single-scale view of anything. The model only worked because it was multiscale. If you tried to describe the picture at one level of granularity, you'd always miss something that people obviously saw. And that turns out to be true for understanding neural networks too. You want the big picture of what a model is doing, and you want the fine-grained mechanics, and the interesting stuff is usually how those levels connect. So in a funny way, that old perception project set me up to think about interpretability in a way I didn't expect at the time.

r001.rationale: The response describes a multiscale model of visual grouping, but does not identify computer-vision scale-space techniques or say they formalize designers’ intuitions.

r002.rationale: It discusses differences between data and perception, but does not say Wattenberg’s understanding of vision at the time was insufficient to simulate the viewing experience.

r003.rationale: It mentions showing images and collecting what people reported, but does not compare that with briefly talking to someone and observing their use of a visualization.

astra-6.text:
It taught me that understanding a visualization isn’t just a matter of decoding individual marks. We often talk about whether people can accurately compare two lengths or distinguish two colors, and those are useful questions. But before you do any of that, you organize what you’re seeing. You see groups, boundaries, and patterns, often at several scales.

Think about a scatterplot. At one level, you’re looking at individual points. At another, you see clusters. At another, you see the overall shape of the data. A relationship that’s obvious at one scale can disappear at another. So the question becomes: what structure does the visualization make available, and how does someone move between those levels?

For me, the lesson was that we need to study that organization alongside accuracy on simple tasks. A visualization helps people understand data partly by helping them decide what counts as a meaningful thing to look at.

sol-6.1.text:
It taught me to be careful about thinking of a visualization as a collection of individual marks. We often talk as if someone looks at a chart, reads off a few values, and then reasons about them. But a lot happens before that. You see groups, boundaries, patterns—you organize the image at different scales.

Take a scatterplot. At one scale you might see a single cloud; at another, several clusters; and at another, individual points that don’t fit. Those are different ways of understanding the same picture, and people move between them depending on what they’re trying to find out.

So for me, the lesson was that understanding a visualization means understanding that perceptual organization, as well as the task. It’s not enough to ask whether a particular value is encoded accurately. You also have to ask what structures people will see, and whether those structures help them ask and answer useful questions.
